name: Botox nose tip lift

lead: A Botox nose tip lift relaxes the depressor septi nasi, a small muscle that tugs the nasal tip downward. Proponents say this lets a drooping tip sit a little higher, especially one that drops further when smiling or speaking.

Botulinum toxin blocks the signal from nerve to muscle, weakening the targeted muscle for a period of months, which reduces its downward pull on the tip. Effects are reported to last roughly two to four months, sometimes up to six. No clinical trials of the nasal tip use were located, so the size and duration of the effect are documented as practitioner claims.

paras: It is done in a clinic by an injector as a short-term alternative to surgery, and sometimes grouped with other non-surgical nose treatments. The effect fades as the toxin wears off, so users repeat it if they want to keep the look.

Botulinum toxin is prescription-only. Reported cosmetic adverse effects include weakness of nearby muscles, headache and allergic reactions, and the FDA has issued warnings about toxin spreading beyond the injection site. The nasal use is off-label, as cosmetic approvals concern glabellar (frown) lines.

angle.text: Proponents use botulinum toxin in the depressor septi nasi muscle as a short-term way to lift a drooping nasal tip, especially one that drops when smiling. Relaxing the muscle reduces its downward pull so the tip sits slightly higher. It is an off-label use with temporary results, and no published trials were located.

lead: A Botox nose tip lift is a cosmetic procedure in which botulinum toxin is injected into the depressor septi nasi, a small muscle that pulls the nasal tip and the base of the nostrils downward. Relaxing it lets the tip rest slightly higher, which people use to lift a tip that droops, particularly one that drops further when they smile or talk. It is described by proponents as a short-term, non-surgical alternative to rhinoplasty [1][2].

The depressor septi nasi originates near the upper jaw and inserts into the nasal septum and the alar part of the nasalis muscle; it also moves the nasal tip when the upper lip moves [1]. It is one of the facial muscles of the nose, alongside the procerus and nasalis [2]. Botulinum toxin products are prescription-only in the US, UK and EU, and cosmetic effects are reported to last roughly two to four months, sometimes up to six [3].

The nasal tip use is off-label: the cosmetic approval in the US concerns glabellar (frown) lines.[3] A 2024 systematic review of botulinum toxin for nasal aesthetics, which included 23 of 1,139 screened articles, reports that the toxin can address drooping nasal tips, dilated nostrils and high columellar show, and calls it a safe and effective option for minor nasal defects while recommending larger studies.[4] In the broader non-surgical rhinoplasty field, dermal fillers are the usual tool for lifting a drooping tip or raising the bridge.[5]

paras: The depressor septi nasi pulls the nasal tip and columella downward and narrows the nostrils, acting as an antagonist to other nasal muscles [1]. Practitioners say that relaxing it reduces the downward pull so a tip that dips on smiling appears less drooped. Wikipedia's muscle entry notes only that surgeons reposition its head during rhinoplasty to help ensure normal nose position afterward and does not discuss toxin treatment [1].

Cosmetic use of botulinum toxin was first described in 1989 and the FDA approved Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines in 2002. Smoothing generally appears within several days and peaks around one week [3]. Reported adverse effects in cosmetic use include unintended weakness of nearby muscles, headache, flu-like symptoms and allergic reactions; the FDA issued warnings in 2008 and added boxed warnings in 2009 concerning spread of toxin beyond the injection site [3].

sections.h: Technique and uses in nasal esthetics
paras: The 2024 systematic review lists three main nasal indications for toxin: a drooping tip pulled down by the depressor septi nasi, widened or flared nostrils (alar muscle activity) and excessive columellar show.[4] A narrative review of cosmetic toxin treatment in the oral and maxillofacial area likewise describes injection sites and techniques for the lower face and discusses differences between Asian and Caucasian patients and the use of ultrasound guidance.[4]

Toxin is also used around rhinoplasty. A 2021 comparison of 30 patients who received toxin after corrective rhinoplasty with 30 controls reported lower postoperative deviation in the toxin group, vertical 0.20 degrees versus 1.20 and horizontal 0.80 versus 2.18, and the authors said the toxin restricted the paranasal muscles without significant adverse events.[4]

Non-surgical rhinoplasty usually means filler injection, which can raise a flat bridge, lift a drooping tip and smooth bumps but only adds volume. Hyaluronic acid fillers last about 6 to 10 months and can be dissolved with hyaluronidase; calcium hydroxyapatite lasts about 10 to 14 months and cannot be reversed. The most serious filler risk described is accidental injection into an artery, causing skin necrosis or rarely vision loss [5]. A toxin tip lift differs in that it relaxes a muscle rather than adding volume.
The evidence base consists of a systematic review, small clinical series and combination-treatment studies rather than large randomised trials of the tip lift alone.

The 2024 systematic review in the Indian Journal of Otolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery searched four databases through May 2023, included 23 articles and concluded that botulinum toxin is a safe and effective option for minor nasal defects such as a drooping tip, while calling for larger studies.[4]

A 2025 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology compared three non-surgical rhinoplasty combinations in 85 patients using FACE-Q nose scores at one month and one year. The combination of barbed threads, hyaluronic acid filler and botulinum toxin A had the highest satisfaction and the smallest decline over time; adverse effects appeared in all groups at 48 hours and had fully resolved by one week.[4] Because toxin was one part of a combination, the study does not isolate its effect on the tip.
The 2021 post-rhinoplasty comparison in 60 patients (30 with toxin, 30 controls) is described above.[4]

The procedure appears in lists of non-surgical nose treatments as a way to lift a drooping tip without surgery, presented as a temporary adjustment that wears off as the toxin effect fades. It is often mentioned with fillers and threads as part of a 'liquid rhinoplasty' menu. Practitioners generally describe it as best suited to a tip that droops mainly on animation.

Botulinum toxin products are prescription-only in the US, UK and EU, and the cosmetic market is dominated by branded products; Wikipedia gives 1989 as the first description of cosmetic use and 2002 as the US approval of Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines.[3] An Italian expert consensus published in 2026 on high-dose incobotulinumtoxinA in a full-face approach, funded by the manufacturer Merz Aesthetics Italia, illustrates how toxin protocols are increasingly extended across the face using electromyographic guidance.[4]
